name: Specter Veil
geological_features: An upper atmosphere of near-transparent hydrogen that makes the planet appear ghostly from orbit
Deep atmospheric layers of ammonia and phosphine creating internal cloud decks
A small rocky core surrounded by layers of compressed exotic ices
specific_features: Electromagnetic signatures in the deep atmosphere that briefly mimic the patterns of nearby vessels before fading
description: Specter Veil earns its name from a quirk of atmospheric chemistry that makes it nearly invisible against the backdrop of space. Its outer atmosphere is composed of hydrogen so pure and sparse that it is essentially transparent, allowing starlight to pass through without significant scattering. The planet reveals itself only at depth, where ammonia and phosphine cloud decks form ghostly internal structures visible as faint luminous shapes hanging in apparent void. From a distance, it looks less like a planet than a haunting.

Navigating near Specter Veil requires constant instrument reference, as visual observation is unreliable. The transparent outer layers create optical illusions where the internal cloud structures appear to be at different distances and scales than they actually are, and the planet's gravitational influence extends well beyond its visible presence. Pilots report the disorienting experience of instruments warning of proximity to a massive body while their eyes see only stars and the faint glow of deep clouds.

The electromagnetic mimicry is the planet's most studied and least explained phenomenon. Brief radio frequency bursts matching the emission profiles of nearby vessels have been detected emanating from the deep atmosphere, delayed by minutes or hours and subtly distorted. The effect has been attributed to atmospheric lensing and re-emission, but the precision of the mimicry exceeds what simple reflection should produce. Some researchers have proposed a natural plasma phenomenon that temporarily stores and replays electromagnetic patterns.

Helium-3 harvesting at Specter Veil is complicated by the navigation hazards and the psychological toll on crews who spend weeks stationed near a world they cannot reliably see. The ghost signals add to the unease, particularly when they reproduce communications that the crew recognizes as their own transmissions from hours earlier. Automated harvesting systems have proven more practical, though even these occasionally respond to the mimic signals as though receiving legitimate commands.
